13-39.title: After an injury while helping, use the legal compensation routes — there is no automatic reimbursement fund
13-39.inPlainWords: If you are injured while saving someone, you may have a claim against the person who caused the danger, a claim under the Motor Vehicles Act for a road accident, or victim compensation under the BNSS, 2023. The Good Samaritan protection in section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act protects you from liability; it does not pay your bill. Keep the medical records and the police report.
13-39.benefit: Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 protects a Good Samaritan from civil and criminal liability for helping a road-accident victim. The BNSS, 2023 provides victim compensation, and the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 provides legal aid. A civil suit in tort can claim damages from the wrongdoer. A government hospital must provide emergency treatment.
13-39.cost: Emergency treatment at a government hospital is free or low cost. A private hospital bill is recoverable only through a claim.
13-39.caveats: A rescue does not create an automatic state-funded payout. Preserve the police report, the medical records and the witness details. A claim has a limitation period.

13-2.cost: No money is required. Kneeling down to ask a few questions and making a phone call takes only a few minutes. The hard part is resisting the urge to reach out and help. For strangers, there is an extra cost to consider: calling 112 leaves your number on the emergency-service record, which may result in follow-up calls or inquiries. If family members later target you, legal battles can last months, and even if you ultimately win, you will still have to pay your own legal fees.
13-2.caveats: This grade is assigned because the guidelines describe proper procedures but provide no quantitative data on how many lives they actually save. Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 protects a Good Samaritan who helps a road-accident victim from civil and criminal liability, but it does not cover moving an injured person unnecessarily, so waiting for 112 remains the safer choice. After dialing 112, stay on the line and follow the dispatcher's instructions. This advice is primarily intended for one's own elderly relatives and acquaintances. For strangers on the street, walking away is legal: Indian law creates no general duty to rescue a stranger. That said, once you stop, you must weigh all associated costs: time spent, leaving your contact details, contact potential from family members, possible legal action, workplace repercussions, and even online backlash. For fall prevention, refer to Section 1, Item 13 (balance and leg-strength training); delayed symptoms following head trauma are covered in Section 10; financial recourse after injury sustained while rescuing others is addressed in Section 39; and evidence collection and reporting in cases of online harassment are outlined in Section 8, Item 16.

13-2.benefit: If they’re vomiting, turn their head to one side and clear any vomit from their mouth and nose. If breathing or heartbeat has stopped, start chest compressions at once. The guidelines also note: “If moving the person is necessary, do so gently and keep them as flat as possible.” For conscious individuals, ask whether they recall the fall; if not, it may indicate fainting or a cerebrovascular event. If they suffer severe headaches, facial drooping, slurred speech, or limb weakness, lifting them could worsen bleeding or ischemia in the brain. Likewise, if there are signs of fracture, back pain, or incontinence, avoid moving them unless you have relevant medical training. In all these cases, call 112 immediately. If the elderly person wishes to stand up on their own, assist them slowly, then let them sit or lie down while you monitor them until you’re sure they’re alright. Conversely, Indian law protects the rescuer rather than paying him. Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 says that a Good Samaritan is not liable for any civil or criminal action for the injury or death of an accident victim caused by the rescuer’s negligence while giving emergency care or carrying the victim to hospital, and it defines a Good Samaritan as a person acting in good faith, voluntarily and “without expectation of any reward or compensation”. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Good Samaritan guidelines of 12 May 2015, issued on the direction of the Supreme Court in SaveLIFE Foundation v. Union of India, add that a bystander who takes an injured person to hospital must be allowed to leave at once and is not to be questioned, that a person who telephones the police or the emergency services cannot be compelled to reveal his name or details, and that a rescuer who volunteers as an eyewitness is examined on a single occasion. What the law does not provide is money: any reward is left to the state government to specify, so no payout is guaranteed, and there is no right to compensation for injured ribs or lost hours. Section 134A is written for road accidents; for a fall inside a home it does not apply, and what protects you there is that Indian law imposes no duty to rescue a stranger.

caveats: Calling 120 instead of driving is essential because ambulances transport patients directly to stroke centers where staff can be alerted in advance.

13-37.title: If you come across a group fight, walk away — do not try to break it up, do not stand and watch, and do not pick anything up from the ground. If you want the police involved, retreat to a safe distance and call 112.
13-37.cost: No money is required. The hard part is resisting the urge to step in and the temptation to watch from the sidelines. After you call, the police may ask you to give a statement later; at most, this takes half a day.
13-37.inPlainWords: If you step in, you stop being a bystander: under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 you can end up as one of the people accused of rioting or of causing hurt, and meaning to calm things down is not a defence. Watching is not worth it either — the more onlookers there are, the messier the scene gets, and the more likely you are to be hurt. The right move is to walk away. If you do want the police involved, step back to a safe spot and dial 112, stating the location, how many people are involved, whether anyone is carrying knives or sticks, and whether anyone is on the ground.
13-37.benefit: Serious fights are investigated as rioting, unlawful assembly, hurt and, where someone dies, culpable homicide under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 the police must record information about a cognizable offence (section 173), and a First Information Report can be lodged at any police station, including one outside the area where the fight happened, so you do not have to find the right jurisdiction first. A caller who gives the location, the number of people and the weapons has given the police what they need; you do not have to stay at the scene.
13-37.caveats: This is graded B because the consequences are set out in statutes, but the advice to walk away rather than intervene is derived from them rather than stated as a rule. Saying "I was only trying to mediate" is not a defence; what matters is whether you took part and whom you hit. If an attacker is already down or has fled, chasing them to hit them is no longer private defence. The law does allow reasonable force in private defence of yourself or another person under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but a bare-handed intervention usually just adds another casualty. Calling 112, recording from a distance and staying out of the fight are more effective. There is no statutory duty on a passer-by to step in. If you are later asked to give a statement, tell the truth; fabricating an account, or helping someone hide, is itself an offence. The benefit of calling 112 mainly helps the person on the ground, and overall this entry offers one of the lowest net benefits in the book. If you yourself get caught in a fight, see Section 8, Item 10; if a stranger demands money, see Item 36 of this section; for costs after helping an injured person, see Item 39.

13-27.title: If you are lost or stranded in a desert, on a high plateau or in any other remote area, stay put next to your vehicle. First transmit your location, then shield yourself from the sun, retain body heat, conserve water and avoid wandering off.
13-27.cost: Before venturing into such areas, tell someone your planned route, destination, return date, vehicle type and registration number. You will need at least 4 litres of water per person per day. A satellite communicator or a personal locator beacon costs thousands of rupees, and rental runs to a few hundred rupees per use. The real challenge is remembering to stay put and not wander away.

13-38.cost: At a government ART centre or a designated hospital under the National AIDS Control Programme, a 28-day course of PEP is normally free. At a private hospital it can cost several thousand rupees. You will need to go that same night. The hardest part is admitting you might be infected and leaving right away.
13-38.benefit: India's National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) defines this as post-exposure prophylaxis, PEP: a 28-day course of antiretroviral drugs started as soon as possible after exposure, ideally within 2 hours and no later than 72 hours. Beyond 72 hours PEP is not advised. PEP is prescribed by a doctor at a government ART centre or a designated hospital. This strict timeline means that acting immediately versus waiting a night can produce completely different outcomes.
13-38.caveats: PEP is stocked at government ART centres and many district hospitals, not at every emergency room, so call ahead first; the ART centre list is published on naco.gov.in, and turning up at the wrong queue can cost you the night. Situations considered "exposures" include unprotected sex, a broken condom, a needle-stick injury or blood contact with mucous membranes; only a doctor can decide whether PEP is appropriate. The full 28-day regimen must be completed; missing doses markedly reduces its effectiveness. Follow-up testing is required at 4-6 weeks and at 3 months as directed by your physician. This is a remedial measure, not a substitute for regular prevention; for everyday safeguards and testing, see items 30 and 31 in Chapter 1 (consistent condom use and testing after high-risk encounters).

13-42.benefit: Indian practice follows the same sequence. The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 requires the police to record information about a cognizable offence, and a zero FIR can be lodged at any police station, including one outside the area where the assault happened. Every hospital, public or private, must give a survivor of sexual violence free first-aid and medical treatment and must inform the police; the forensic examination is done at a government hospital, and a One Stop Centre (Sakhi Centre) run under the Ministry of Women and Child Development can provide a counsellor and accompany you. Preserving evidence is the priority: keep body fluids, hair, skin cells and communication records, and do not shower, wash clothes, tidy the room or throw anything away before the examination. In cases involving acquaintances, preserve call logs and messages, and document any threats or attempts at bribery. WHO notes that emergency contraception may be used when a woman has been sexually assaulted without effective contraceptive protection, recommending its use within five days for maximum effectiveness; the pills work best when taken early, ideally within 72 hours. PEP for HIV should be taken within two hours if possible, and no later than 72 hours.

In stuporous or comatose stages marked by cyanosis, cold extremities, hypothermia and shallow breathing, call 112 immediately, keep the person on their side, cover them with warm blankets, and start CPR if breathing stops.
The same rule holds everywhere: never let an intoxicated person sleep alone, because nobody will notice if their breathing stops.
13-46.caveats: Graded B because the advice rests on official health authority emergency guidance and clinical consensus; India has no statute that places a legal duty on a bystander. Benefit is categorized as High because asphyxiation and respiratory arrest occur almost exclusively when victims are left unmonitored. Never attempt manual throat-tickling emesis on lethargic or unresponsive individuals. Beyond family members, these duties apply heavily to dining companions and colleagues: in India a claim against a drinking companion would have to be brought as a civil negligence suit, so the practical duty is social rather than statutory, but failing to get someone home safely is what turns a bad night into a death. Always escort drunk companions directly into the custody of family or remain until sobriety returns. If you discover an unknown intoxicated person collapsed outdoors, call 112 without attempting forceful repositioning unless necessary (see Chapter 13, Rule 2). Alcohol impairs thermoregulation; manage hypothermia as outlined in Chapter 13, Rule 28. Alcohol interactions with cephalosporin or metronidazole antibiotics causing disulfiram-like reactions are detailed in Chapter 34, Rule 11. Never take hot baths or enter saunas after drinking (see Chapter 22, Rule 11).

13-36.title: If a stranger demands money in a remote area, hand over the cash, avoid a confrontation, note his features and call 112 once you are away — a bare demand is extortion, not robbery
13-36.inPlainWords: Give him the money, do not fight back, do not argue. What he is doing depends on how he does it. A demand with no force and no immediate threat is extortion under section 308 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, punishable with imprisonment of up to seven years, or with fine, or with both; where the demand is backed by fear of death or of grievous hurt, up to ten years and a fine. It becomes robbery under section 309 only when he uses force, or puts you in fear of instant death, instant hurt or instant restraint, and takes the property there and then. Robbery carries rigorous imprisonment of up to ten years and a fine, extended to fourteen years where it is committed on a highway between sunset and sunrise; where hurt is voluntarily caused in the robbery, the punishment is imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment of up to ten years. Dacoity — robbery by five or more people acting together — carries imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment of up to ten years under section 310, and death is available only where one of them commits murder in the dacoity. None of this is a reason to resist. If you chase him once he has taken the money and strike him, that is no longer private defence: the right of private defence in sections 34 to 44 of the Sanhita covers stopping an ongoing attack, not retaliation afterwards. As soon as you are safe, write down his appearance, his accent, the vehicle number and the direction he went, and call 112.
13-36.benefit: Your life is worth far more than a few hundred rupees, and he is risking a long sentence for a small sum. The law’s line is simple. Taking property by force, or by fear of instant harm, is robbery under section 309, and it carries rigorous imprisonment of up to ten years, fourteen on a highway between sunset and sunrise, and imprisonment for life where hurt is voluntarily caused. Robbery by five or more people acting together is dacoity under section 310, punishable with imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment of up to ten years, with death reserved for murder committed in the dacoity. Self-defence is bounded the same way: sections 34 to 44 allow the force needed to stop an ongoing attack, and once the robber has taken the money and walked away, retaliation is a fresh offence rather than defence. Your work afterwards is evidence — his description, his speech, the vehicle, the escape route — and the first information you give at the police station, where section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 requires the information to be recorded.
